newsitem.title: CHINA: Free market not to challenge China condom market.
newsitem.headline: Free market not to challenge China condom market.

text.p: Free market forces have challenged many of China's traditional planned industries such as bicycles, shampoo, televisions and noodles but one product will not be allowed to face competition -- contraceptives.

China fears a free-for-all in sale and distribution of condoms could result in couples lacking access to contraceptives and a country of 1.2 billion people cannot afford contraceptive slip-ups, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday.

"Central planning of the contraceptive-goods production and distribution are necessary as pushing the business into the free market entails an unacceptable risk level," it quoted Li Luyang of the State Family Planning Commission as saying.

"The government attaches importance to the manufacturing and distribution of all needed products for the simple reason that every failure in contraception brings trouble to the couple and the society," said the newspaper quoting Li.

The chances of imports and products made by enterprises not included on the state-appointed list of condom suppliers being distributed through the state system were "zero", it quoted Lin Shaoxu of the Ministry of Chemical Industry as saying.

Since 1988, the Family Planning Commission has set up a chain of contraceptive counters at stores across China. Condoms can also be bought across the counter from neighbourhood grocery stores, the newspaper said.
But most people in China never buy oral contraceptives or condoms -- they are distributed free by employers.

In 1995, China spent 220 million yuan ($26.5 million) on production of 1.17 billion condoms, $4.7 million on birth-control pills and $2.4 million on intra-uterine devices (IUDs), the commission's Li said.
About seven percent of couples use condoms and birth-control pills, while the rest rely on IUDs or sterilisation, Li said.
At least one foreign latex producer is lauching condom production in China, although investors say a major challenge is to win permission for its products to enter the state distribution system.
